The estimator uses calibration estimates, a local feature mean and an empirical recovery feature. The constant is expressed through a bounded-normal decision problem. We verify the conditions in two models. In centered Gaussian logistic errors-in-variables regression with one surrogate and two unknown variances, we determine the fifth-order global coefficient risk and its exact constant. A sparse extension separates variance-decomposition uncertainty from direction estimation and specifies when the scalar constant is preserved. In a degree-balanced replicated-network model, we determine the sixth-order global edge-contrast risk when block proportions are unknown. Triangles identify a parameter combination; a bowtie supplies the additional information needed for the contrast.

title: Batched NN 4D-Var: a performant hybrid model framework for the Integrated Forecasting System
summary: Hybrid forecasting systems combining machine learning and numerical weather prediction offer a promising route toward improved forecast skill while preserving physical consistency. In this study, we investigate online learning of state-dependent model-error corrections within the Integrated Forecasting System using 4D-Var. Building on previous work, we represent model error using a neural network embedded within the forecast model and trained from observations through the data assimilation cycle. First, we introduce a targeted variant of neural-network 4D-Var in which only the neural-network parameters are estimated, while the atmospheric state is provided by a precomputed analysis. We then propose a batched extension that processes assimilation windows in random order and averages parameter increments over multiple windows, drawing inspiration from mini-batch stochastic optimization. Experiments are conducted with the Integrated Forecasting System of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts at an intermediate resolution. Sequential online learning substantially improves forecasts within the training period, with error reductions exceeding 10%in some cases. However, these improvements fail to generalize to unseen data. In contrast, the proposed batched formulation produces hybrid models that consistently improve forecast skill in out-of-sample experiments. Larger batch sizes accelerate convergence and improve robustness by reducing the noise of parameter updates. Diagnostics further show that the online-trained corrections preserve realistic forecast variability and do not improve skill through artificial smoothing. These results demonstrate that the formulation of the online learning problem is critical for generalisation and establish batched online training as a promising framework for hybrid machine-learning/data-assimilation systems.

title: Let's Do Turbulence Right: In Space and Time!
summary: The three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations govern fluid turbulence, a chaotic and non-linear physical phenomenon characterized by complex eddies interacting across vast spatial and temporal scales. A numerically accurate modeling of this multi-scale energy cascade requires fully resolving both the fine spatial structures and the continuous temporal evolution of the flow field. In this paper, we leverage massive, time-resolved direct numerical simulations, which exceed 28 TB per run, to assess how numerical choices govern the resolved (3+1)-dimensional physics of turbulent flows. Building on this analysis, we study how neural networks represent the recorded turbulent motion. Our results highlight that spatial and temporal assessments can disagree for both numerical records and learned representations. We therefore call on the machine learning community to treat (3+1)-dimensional turbulence as a four-dimensional phenomenon.

title: Acquisition for Spherical-Linear Bayesian Optimization on the Cube
summary: Recent work demonstrated that executing Bayesian Optimization (BO) using simply a linear surrogate with a clever transformation is enough to approximate the performance of the standard Gaussian-Process (GP) based version on high-dimensional test functions. When the decision region is a sphere, this strategy admits rapid exact acquisition. However, it is the unit cube we encounter most often in the BO literature, and in this setting a standard approach, namely a multi-start quasi-Newton method, is employed for solving the acquisition subproblem. In this article, we will discuss a series of results, both positive and negative, regarding the complexity of global resolution of various acquisition subproblems over the unit cube. On the basis of this discussion, we will propose a new acquisition function which is globally optimizable using significantly less execution time than the incumbent approach while maintaining or improving performance. The resulting method is competitive with GP-based BO in terms of accuracy per evaluation, and is superior in terms of accuracy per walltime on black-boxes of low to moderate computational intensity.

title: Computational imaging through turbid, bubbly and flowing water near the telescope
summary: Cameras in the surf zone or behind ship wakes look through turbid, bubbly, moving water close to the lens, yet restoration networks are usually scored only on displayed images. We introduce a measured dataset of a telescope viewing displayed images and physical objects through a 25~mm water layer 45~mm in front of its objective, under seven combinations of flow, bubbles and turbidity, with clear-water recordings as a second reference. Because the suspension scatters light far outside the 1.3\textdegree{} field of view, turbidity mainly removes contrast, 4.4- to 4.8-fold on a Siemens star. Restoring the mean of eight frames improves structural similarity (SSIM) by 0.032 over a single frame, and learned fusion of the frames adds little. One raw frame supports five-category recognition (96.8\%) as well as restored images. Adding synthetic training pairs leaves display-image scores unchanged but raises the correlation of a restored Siemens star with its clear-water recording from below 0.5 to above 0.9. These networks also improve ordinary underwater photographs without retraining, where training on measured pairs alone fails. Scoring against the digital source or a clear-water recording reverses the ranking of raw and restored images. These results support a simple pipeline: average the frames, classify raw frames directly, and restore with networks trained on measured and synthetic pairs.

title: Sensitivity-Guided Parameter Estimation of Bubbly Liquid via a Nonlinear Wave Equation and Physics-InformedNeuralNetworks
summary: Interactions between ultrasound and microbubbles underlie a range of biomedical and industrial applications, yet predicting how the physical parameters of the medium and bubbles govern nonlinear wave propagation remains difficult. This study proposes a parameter estimation framework that combines a Korteweg-de Vries-Burgers (KdVB) equation, describing weakly nonlinear wave propagation in a bubbly liquid, with a physics-informed neural network (PINN). The contributions are threefold. First, the PINN reproduces the reference solution of the governing equation in the forward problem, with a near-zero prediction error at the initial time that confirms the initial condition is enforced exactly as intended. Second, prior to inverse estimation, a sensitivity analysis is introduced that quantifies, at both the coefficient and solution levels, how each of eight physical parameters influences the KdVB equation, allowing the expected difficulty of estimating each parameter to be assessed in advance. Third, based on this assessment, single-parameter inverse estimation is performed for seven of the eight parameters using the PINN. Liquid viscosity, bubble initial radius, liquid density, sound speed, and liquid pressure are estimated with errors of 0.8-2.1%, the polytropic exponent converges only partially, and the surface tension coefficient cannot be estimated at all, consistent with the sensitivity analysis. These results establish a general framework for identifying and estimating the physical parameters governing nonlinear wave propagation in bubbly liquids from observed waveform data.

title: EMG Tokenization Preserves Movement Information at a Fraction of the Bitrate
comments: 11 pages, 7 figures; 12-page supplement included. Supplementary Data 1-9 (CSV) are provided as ancillary files
summary: Wireless electromyography (EMG) interfaces must balance electrode coverage against transmission bandwidth. Here, we show that compact EMG tokens substantially reduce payload while retaining information for three-dimensional hand-pose decoding. We evaluate two causal tokenizers fitted without pose labels: an encoder pretrained to reconstruct EMG spectra and one based on SPAR, an engineered spectral-spatial representation of neighbouring electrodes. In personalized, within-session experiments with 320-channel EMG from nine participants, we compare tokenized and continuous features using matched decoder architectures and training procedures. Averaged across decoders, tokenization changed mean error by +0.01 mm for SPAR (95% confidence interval: -0.12 to 0.14) and +0.45 mm for the learned representation (0.10 to 0.82). Both increases met a 1 mm non-inferiority criterion. Stored token arrays reduced payloads 41-fold relative to raw EMG and 36-fold relative to continuous SPAR features. On sampled windows of the public emg2pose benchmark's test partition, absolute differences in mean error between learned tokens and continuous features were below 0.05 mm across 176 participants and in the subset of 20 participants unseen during training. Electrode coverage, calibration, and unseen recordings affected SPAR decoding more than quantization did. In a computational benchmark, optimized SPAR generated tokens for 63 channels within 20 ms on a Cortex-M55 microcontroller. These findings support tokenization as a compact interface between wearable sensing and movement decoding, allowing decoders to be updated while the wearable encoder and transmitted representation remain fixed.
comment: 11 pages, 7 figures; 12-page supplement included. Supplementary Data 1-9 (CSV) are provided as ancillary files

title: Probing the limits of forward screening and inverse design of crystal materials
summary: Crystal materials are designed either by screening known crystals for a target property or by generating new crystals with that property. Both routes are judged against public databases of known crystals, but these databases name the same crystal differently. Several materials announced as new by recent generative and autonomous discovery campaigns have since proved to be known phases or close variants of them. The limits of both routes remain unmeasured. Here we probe them by matching the crystals of 55 databases by structure into one self-extending database of 14.6 million crystals and 131.8 million property values, each traced to its source. Only 4.5% of its crystal-property pairs carry a value. To fill the empty pairs, we developed CGTNet, an equivariant graph transformer with state-of-the-art accuracy on several tasks of two public benchmarks. Trained on each task, it forms a library of property models whose predictions we release. The reach of forward screening has been underestimated. Known crystals hold tens of thousands of ultra-incompressible candidates without a recorded bulk modulus, and a post hoc audit of synthesis evidence finds among them ReN2, whose bulk modulus was measured at 428 GPa. The novelty claimed for inverse design has been overestimated. At an equal verification budget, a stiffness-conditioned generator returned more stiff hits than screening (100 versus 55), but all contained osmium and 82 repeated recorded compositions. Integrating and completing the databases of known crystals therefore moves the limits of both routes: it widens what screening can reach and sets the reference against which generated crystals are judged new.

title: Superlinear Convergence of Cyclic Gradient Methods with Historical Ritz Step Sizes
summary: Simplified spectral models predict dimension-dependent superlinear convergence for gradient methods, but the corresponding behavior of actual iterations remains only partially understood. Historical methods introduce an additional difficulty: the gradients defining the step sizes differ from those receiving them. We study this offset for cyclic reuse of historical Ritz step sizes on strictly convex quadratics. Within the existing limited memory steepest descent with retards (LMSDR) family, a rolling cyclic Ritz (RCR) rule reuses $m$ historical Ritz values $\ell$ times per cycle, ending with a complete sweep. At $q=m+1$ active distinct eigenvalues, an exact delayed recurrence gives almost-everywhere doubly exponential convergence with an explicit rate and exceptional weights. Nonempty open basins also exist for $m+1<q\le2m$ and $\ell\ge4$. Rebuilding the history from each cycle-start gradient costs $m$ additional updates and gives sampled cyclic Ritz reuse (SCR) a cycle-end map determined by the current weights. Under uniform sampling bounds, SCR converges doubly exponentially almost everywhere when $(2\ell-1)^m>\binom{q-1}{m}$. Increasing $\ell$ admits larger $q$ for fixed $m$. The guarantee extends to history-dependent choices from finite sampling menus under a bound on the number of admissible sampling sequences. Geometrically spaced decisions retain the SCR condition and rate range. Every update is counted, including sampling; a numerical illustration compares finite-tolerance update counts.

title: Score-Preserving Continual Lasso under Task Shift
summary: Continual learning (CL) aims to learn from sequential tasks while mitigating catastrophic forgetting when historical data are no longer accessible. We study continual learning for high-dimensional sparse linear regression, where $\ell_1$ regularization creates a difficulty absent from continual ridge regression: that recursively reusing an $\ell_1$-penalized estimator can propagate earlier shrinkage and accumulate regularization bias across tasks. We propose score-preserving continual Lasso (SP-CL), which separates sparse estimation from state transmission by preserving the historical squared-loss score. Under squared loss, its cumulative estimator exactly recovers a full-history Lasso minimizer. When task coefficients coincide, it inherits the full-history sparse rate. For related task-specific coefficients, SP-CL uses a regularized current-task correction that leaves the transmitted state unchanged and attains the offline source-assisted rate under an oracle related-task condition. We also derive Overall/BWT/FWT decompositions that distinguish historical information loss, task conflict, and current-task specialization, and validate the resulting regimes in simulation.

title: The Butterfly Defects: Tracing Cooperation in LLM Agent Networks
summary: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly operate as interconnected agents, a fundamental question emerges: does individual cooperation translate into collective cooperation? We investigate this question through the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma (IPD), moving from dyadic interactions to homogeneous and heterogeneous networks of open-weight LLMs. Our findings reveal that cooperation is highly sensitive to model composition and seemingly minor linguistic changes. Models that cooperate with identical peers can shift toward defection in mixed populations. A simple uncertainty cue can increase or decrease cooperation, redistribute costs, and affect unexposed agents several hops away. Even reversing action-label order can dramatically alter behavior, with uncertainty framing sometimes amplifying this sensitivity. Together, these findings challenge the notion of cooperation as a stable model-level property, revealing how strategic behavior depends on interaction partners, network positions, and the language used to frame decisions.

title: A probabilistic construction of maximum $h$-scattered subspaces
summary: Let $1\le h\le n-2$ and $g=\gcd(n,h+1)$. We prove that, for every prime power $q$, a maximum $h$-scattered $\mathbb{F}_q$-subspace of $V(r,q^n)$ exists whenever $(h+1)\mid rn$ and $$r\ge\frac{h+1}{g}\bigl(h(n-h-2)+1\bigr).$$ In particular, for fixed $n$ and minimum distance $δ\in\{2,\ldots,n-1\}$, $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$-linear MRD codes of length $N$ exist for every $q$ and every sufficiently large $N$ such that $n$ divides $(n-δ+1)N$, with a bound on $N$ depending only on $n$ and $δ$. We take the $\mathbb{F}_{q^s}$-span of the columns of a random matrix $A$ over the algebra $R=\mathbb{F}_{q^n}\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_q}\mathbb{F}_{q^s}$, for a suitable $s$. Such a subspace is maximum $h$-scattered if and only if the kernel of $A$ contains no nonzero vector whose expansion with respect to an $\mathbb{F}_q$-basis of $\mathbb{F}_{q^s}$ has rank weight at most $h+1$. When $\gcd(n,s)=1$, $R$ is a field, and a first-moment argument, counting these vectors up to multiplication by $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}^*\mathbb{F}_{q^s}^*$, shows that with positive probability the kernel contains none of them if $s>h(n-h-2)$. When $d=\gcd(n,s)>1$, $R$ is a product of $d$ fields, and vectors vanishing in some factors lie in the kernel with larger probability. We control them by proving that, for an $(h+1)$-dimensional $\mathbb{F}_q$-subspace $D$ of $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$, the elements of $D\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_q}\mathbb{F}_{q^s}$ vanishing outside $k$ given factors, $0<k<d$, form an $\mathbb{F}_{q^s}$-space of dimension at most $(h+1)k/d$, with equality only if $D$ is linear over a subfield of $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ larger than $\mathbb{F}_q$. Taking $s=gr/(h+1)$ gives the bound on $r$. Finally, if $(n-h-1)\mid(h+1)$, then for every $r$ satisfying the above inequality there is an $h$-scattered $\mathbb{F}_q$-subspace of $V(r,q^n)$ of dimension $\lfloor rn/(h+1)\rfloor$, without a divisibility condition on $rn$.

title: Sparse Bayesian Neural Networks via Sticky Piecewise Deterministic Markov Processes
summary: There is growing evidence that the performance of a neural network depends largely on a small subset of its weights, which are typically identified by training a dense network and pruning it afterwards. Within a Bayesian framework, pruning can be directly incorporated through a spike-and-slab prior, providing a proper treatment of the uncertainties involved, both with respect to pruning and to parameter uncertainty. In Bayesian neural networks (BNNs), sampling by MCMC is notoriously hard. We demonstrate that modern Monte Carlo methods based on piecewise deterministic Markov processes (PDMPs) can be used to sample posteriors of BNNs asymptotically exact whenever numerically constructed rate bounds hold. Spike-and-slab priors can be incorporated through sticky versions of the PDMPs, setting weights exactly to zero during sampling. We examine the predictive performance and convergence of the samplers, and show that sparse BNNs sampled this way can be more robust to input noise than dense ones.

title: ARENA: Active Region attENtion Aggregation for interpretable solar flare prediction
comments: 7+12 pages (2+8 figures), accepted at the "Representations for the Physical Sciences" workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Predicting solar flares is a challenging space-weather forecasting problem with potentially significant impacts on Earth's upper atmosphere, including disruptions to radio communications. We propose Active Region attENtion Aggregation (ARENA), a neural network architecture that predicts solar flares from a variable number of active-region cutouts while learning to identify the region most relevant to the prediction. ARENA is trained using multiple-instance learning under weak supervision, requiring only a flare/no-flare label for the observation and no labels specifying the flare origin. The learned attention mechanism therefore provides a means of localizing the active region driving the prediction without explicit origin annotations. ARENA achieves a heidke skill score of 0.45 which is comparable to other flare prediction approaches. These results demonstrate that active-region-based aggregation can provide an efficient and interpretable approach to solar flare prediction. The code is available at https://github.com/LuisBauer22/ARENA.
comment: 7+12 pages (2+8 figures), accepted at the "Representations for the Physical Sciences" workshop at NeurIPS 2026

title: Generalization properties of the token perceptron: the role of embedding and vocabulary
summary: Large language models are trained to predict tokens from a finite vocabulary, each represented by a vector in a $d$-dimensional embedding space. Therefore, token prediction is a classification problem whose classes have a geometry determined by the embedding. We study how this geometry affects learning in a minimal solvable model: a linear predictor that maps a sequence of $N$ embedded tokens to a $d$-dimensional output through one $d\times d$ matrix per position, trained in the teacher--student setting. We call this the \textit{token perceptron}. We compute its generalization error with the replica method, taking $N\to\infty$ at fixed number of examples per position $α=P/N$ and keeping $d$ and the vocabulary size $D$ finite. As a first reference case, we consider continuous embeddings on the sphere, which isolate the role of the embedding dimension. The natural load is then $α/d$, and for $d>1$ a normalized label fixes the direction of the teacher output, so the problem becomes a noiseless regression: the teacher is recovered exactly above $α_{\rm rec}=d^2/(d-1)$, and spherical cross-entropy reaches this threshold at large inverse temperature. In the same setting the storage capacity of random associations scales as $d^2$ for margins $O(1/\sqrt{d})$. We then turn to vocabulary embeddings, where a label only identifies the Voronoi cell of the teacher output, so that each example imposes inequalities rather than equations, as in the classical perceptron. We compute the Bayes-optimal error for a given embedding matrix through an approximate spectral closure and show that the optimal learner first resolves the directions in which the vocabulary has the largest variance, even when the teacher is isotropic.

title: Proximity Theorem and FPT Algorithm for Minimum Group-labeled Matroid Bases
summary: Let $M$ be a matroid, let $\ell:E(M)\to G$ be a labeling of its elements by an abelian group, and let $F\subseteq G$ be finite. A base is $F$-avoiding if the label sum of its elements is not in $F$. We prove that, for arbitrary costs, a min-cost $F$-avoiding base can be obtained from any min-cost base using at most $|F|$ exchanges. This resolves the weighted proximity conjecture by Hörsch, Imolay, Mizutani, Oki, and Schwarcz. Our main technical tool is to replace the assumption of Schrijver--Seymour Conjecture in Liu and Xu's earlier work with Kemperman--Scherk Theorem. The proximity theorem combined with approaches in earlier work gives an FPT algorithm that finds a min-cost $F$-avoiding base parameterized by $|G|$. We additionally give an FPT algorithm parameterized by $|F|$, answering a question of Hörsch et al.

title: Hardware-Friendly Estimation of LCU-Based Expectation Values via Quantum-to-Classical Workload Shifting
summary: Estimating the expectation value of an observable $O$ for a quantum state evolved under a general, possibly non-unitary, operator $A$ is a fundamental task in quantum simulation, chemistry, and variational algorithms. Existing linear-combination-of-unitaries (LCU) approaches implement $A$ on hardware, requiring ancilla qubits, controlled unitaries and, in randomized variants, fresh circuit executions for every Monte Carlo sample. These costs are prohibitive on NISQ and early fault-tolerant devices. We propose HERMES (Hardware-Efficient Reusable Measurements for Estimating LCU-based expectation valueS), which moves the processing of $A$ entirely to the classical domain. Expanding $A$ and $O$ in the Pauli basis and sampling pairs of Pauli terms classically, HERMES rewrites $μ= \mathrm{Tr}(OAρA^{\dagger})/\mathrm{Tr}(AρA^{\dagger})$ as a ratio of weighted sums of Pauli expectation values on the unmodified state $ρ$, with no ancillas, controlled unitaries, or quantum implementation of $A$. A two-level measurement reduction scheme (Pauli deduplication and commuting-group partitioning) bounds the number of distinct measurement settings independently of the sample count, unlike randomized LCU methods whose circuit executions grow linearly with it. On ground-state energy estimation of $\mathrm{H}_2$ and $\mathrm{LiH}$ via imaginary-time evolution, HERMES matches or beats Pauli single-ancilla LCU baseline using shallow circuits with no two-qubit gates beyond state preparation under qubit-wise commuting grouping. It is also more robust to noise and completes a noisy $\mathrm{LiH}$ simulation infeasible for the baseline, at the cost of classical overhead growing with the number of Pauli terms in $A$.

title: Singular Geometry of Low-Rank Adaptation
summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is now a standard approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks. Its low-rank factorization is inherently non-identifiable, making LoRA a singular statistical model whose learning complexity cannot be described by parameter dimension alone. We study this complexity using the real log canonical threshold (RLCT) from singular learning theory and how it depends on both the low-rank parameterization and the pretrained network. Under a local linearization, LoRA induces a low-rank trace regression model whose Kullback--Leibler geometry is controlled by a forward-backward covariance, constructed from activations and backpropagated sensitivities at the adapted layer. This covariance determines which low-rank perturbations are statistically observable. When it is nondegenerate along the relevant low-rank directions, we recover the classical learning complexity of reduced-rank regression; when its kernel meets these directions, additional statistically indistinguishable parameters change the singular geometry. We characterize this geometry locally through observable tangent directions and a residual singularity, and globally through affine linear sections of determinantal varieties. The global learning complexity need not be determined at a ground-truth parameter, as singularities on another rank stratum can dominate. We also introduce a curvature-corrected multi-temperature estimator of the RLCT. Experiments on multilayer perceptron and transformer architectures reveal strongly layer-dependent forward-backward geometry and show that ambient covariance degeneracy does not imply degeneracy along the low-rank directions relevant to adaptation.

title: Variance of relative entropy over random states
summary: Average relative entropy over major generic random states is recently studied. In this work, the investigation is extended by deriving the variances of relative entropy over the Hilbert--Schmidt and Bures--Hall ensembles, which characterize its fluctuations around the average value. Exact results for the variances of relative entropy between independent states drawn from the same ensemble and from two different ensembles are obtained. These results further indicate that the average relative entropy is typical in the considered limiting regimes. In addition to the matrix-level calculations similar to the average relative entropy, eigenvalue correlation functions of the ensembles are involved in the variance computations through the use of zonal polynomials.

title: Monetizing Intelligence: Advertising and Subscription Design on LLM Platforms
summary: Large language model (LLM) platforms introducing advertising must decide how much capability ad revenue should fund and what consumers should pay to avoid ads. We study a monopolistic platform that jointly chooses costly response quality, advertising intensity, and subscription prices when advertising reduces user value but better service raises advertising returns. Three findings follow. First, when partly ad-supported and ad-free plans coexist, advertising can finance useful service for consumers who receive none under pure subscription. Lower effective quality in middle plans weakens the alternatives available to premium users, allowing higher prices for unchanged ad-free service. Some fully ad-supported users gain utility, while partly ad-supported and ad-free users lose: broader access can coexist with utility polarization. Second, an intermediate advertising cap can maximize consumer surplus by preserving some revenue that finances service while limiting degradation. Third, cheaper compute can raise quality and reduce ad intensity, yet sufficiently large cost reductions can increase aggregate advertising revenue above its initial level because better service raises the value of the remaining advertised interactions. An extension shows how advertising-funded upgrades can bring plans to the same maximum capability and advertising exposure, eliminating the basis for different prices. These results make menu design central to evaluating LLM advertising: the consequences extend beyond users who see ads to the alternatives and prices faced by those who do not.

title: Maximum Likelihood on the Joint (Data, Condition) Distribution for Solving Ill-Posed Problems with Conditional Flow Models
summary: In the absence of conditioning information, normalizing flow models are trained using maximum likelihood. Previous extensions to conditional settings have abandoned the simple maximum-likelihood approach, as obtaining the full joint distribution of data and conditions for training purposes (or equivalently, the true conditional distribution for each point in the training dataset) is impossible. However, under special conditions that nevertheless apply to a wide class of useful problems, it is possible to obtain a simple, computationally cheap proxy with the same global minimum as the conditional likelihood. Conditional flow models trained using this proxy do not require explicit knowledge of the conditional distribution, auxiliary networks or other specific architecture, or additional loss terms beyond maximum likelihood. They provide a natural and powerful way to solve a class of ill-posed inverse problems. I demonstrate these properties on easily visualized toy problems, then use the method to successfully generate class-conditional images and to reconstruct semantically degraded images via super-resolution.

title: FC-PINO: High Precision Physics-Informed Neural Operators via Fourier Continuation
summary: The physics-informed neural operator (PINO) is a machine learning paradigm that has demonstrated promising results for learning solutions to partial differential equations (PDEs). It leverages the Fourier Neural Operator to learn solution operators in function spaces and leverages physics losses during training to penalize deviations from known physics laws. Spectral differentiation provides an efficient way to compute derivatives for the physics losses, but it inherently assumes periodicity. When applied to non-periodic functions, this assumption can lead to significant errors, including Gibbs phenomena near domain boundaries which degrade the accuracy of both function representations and derivative computations. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the FC-PINO (Fourier-Continuation-based Physics-Informed Neural Operator) architecture which extends the accuracy and efficiency of PINO and spectral differentiation to non-periodic and non-smooth PDEs. In FC-PINO, we propose integrating Fourier continuation into the PINO framework, and test two different continuation approaches: FC-Legendre and FC-Gram. By transforming non-periodic signals into periodic functions on extended domains in a well-conditioned manner, Fourier continuation enables fast and accurate derivative computations. This approach avoids the discretization sensitivity of finite differences and the memory overhead of automatic differentiation. We demonstrate that standard PINO fails (without padding) or struggles (even with padding) to solve non-periodic and non-smooth PDEs with high precision, across challenging benchmarks. In contrast, the proposed FC-PINO provides accurate, robust, and scalable solutions, substantially outperforming PINO alternatives, and demonstrating that Fourier continuation is critical for extending PINO to a wider range of PDE problems when high-precision solutions are needed.

title: Extracting total Amb programs from proofs
comments: 39 pages + 4 pages appendix. arXiv admin note: text overlap with arXiv:2104.14669
summary: We present a logical system CFP (Concurrent Fixed Point Logic) supporting the extraction of nondeterministic and concurrent programs that are provably total and correct. CFP is an intuitionistic first-order logic with inductive and coinductive definitions extended by two propositional operators: Restriction (binary), a strengthening of implication, and a unary operator for total concurrency. The source of the extraction is formal CFP proofs, the target is a lambda calculus with constructors and recursion extended by a constructor Amb (for McCarthy's amb) which is interpreted operationally as globally angelic choice and is used to implement nondeterminism and concurrency. The correctness of extracted programs is proven via an intermediate domain-theoretic denotational semantics. We demonstrate the usefulness of our system by extracting a nondeterministic program that translates infinite Gray code into the signed digit representation. A noteworthy feature of CFP is the fact that the proof rules for restriction and concurrency involve variants of the classical law of excluded middle that would not be interpretable computationally without Amb. This is a revised and extended version of the conference paper presented at ESOP 2022 with the same title that contains full proofs of all major results.
comment: 39 pages + 4 pages appendix. arXiv admin note: text overlap with arXiv:2104.14669

title: Learning from Hypervectors: A Survey on Hyperdimensional Encoding
comments: 44 pages, 5 figures, 9 tables. Substantially revised and extended; title updated. Accepted for publication in ACM Computing Surveys (CSUR)
summary: Hyperdimensional computing (HDC) is an emerging computing paradigm that imitates the brain's structure to offer a powerful and efficient processing and learning model. In HDC, the data are encoded with long vectors, called hypervectors, which typically range from 1,000 to 10,000 in length. The literature provides several encoding methods to generate orthogonal or correlated hypervectors, based on the application. Existing surveys focus on overall HDC system aspects like inputs, primary computations, and outputs. However, this study takes a more specific approach. It zeroes in on the HDC system input and the generation of hypervectors, directly influencing the hypervector encoding. This survey brings together various hypervector generation and encoding methods, exploring the limitations, challenges, and potential benefits they entail.
comment: 44 pages, 5 figures, 9 tables. Substantially revised and extended; title updated. Accepted for publication in ACM Computing Surveys (CSUR)

title: On Orthogonal Recurrent Neural Networks Quantization
comments: Progress in Artificial Intelligence, In press
summary: In recent years, Orthogonal Recurrent Neural Networks (ORNNs) have gained popularity due to their ability to manage tasks involving long-term dependencies, such as the Copy-task, and their linear complexity. However, existing ORNNs utilize full precision weights and activations, which prevents their deployment on compact devices. In this paper, we explore the quantization of the weight matrices in ORNNs, leading to Quantized approximately Orthogonal RNNs (QORNNs). The construction of such networks remained an open problem, acknowledged for its inherent instability. We propose and investigate two strategies to learn QORNN by combining quantization-aware training (QAT) and orthogonal projections. We also study post-training quantization of the activations for pure integer computation of the recurrent loop. The most efficient fully-quantized models are currently the only alternatives for solving the Copy-task with 1000 timesteps. They also surpass existing quantized models on tasks requiring long-term dependencies, such as permuted MNIST as well as some Internet of Things (IoT) tasks. However, they are less effective on tasks where long short-term memory (LSTMs) and other gated RNNs outperform ORNNs.
comment: Progress in Artificial Intelligence, In press

title: Puzzle Game: Prediction and Classification of Wordle Solution Words
summary: Wordle result prediction involves both daily participation and the difficulty of the solution word. We model these quantities with ARIMA forecasts of report counts, XGBoost regressors using word frequency, letter entropy, and repetition, and a decision tree trained on K-means difficulty tiers. Experiments use 355 daily outcome distributions, with a 107-word chronological holdout and four expanding-window tests. XGBoost reduces holdout mean absolute error from 4.08 to 3.84 percentage points and improves over the training mean in every temporal window. Ridge and random forests remain competitive. XGBoost systematically underestimates failure rates on difficult words. The lexical decision tree achieves 54.2% tier accuracy, compared with 40.2% when predicted histograms are assigned to the same training centroids. Bootstrap analysis shows that cluster stability does not imply that tiers are predictable from lexical attributes. For report counts, comparisons at matched horizons reveal substantial overdispersion in full-history ARIMA intervals. These results characterize the predictive value and limitations of a compact lexical model of reported Wordle performance.

title: Guard Analysis and Safe Erasure Gradual Typing: a Type System for Elixir
summary:
We formalize a new type system for Elixir, a dynamically typed functional programming language of growing popularity that runs on the Erlang virtual machine. Our system combines gradual typing with semantic subtyping to enable precise, sound, and practical static type analysis, without requiring any changes to Elixir's compilation pipeline or runtime. Type soundness is ensured by leveraging runtime checks -- both implicit, from the Erlang VM, and explicit, via developer-written guards.
  Central to our approach are two key innovations: the notion of "strong functions", which can be assigned precise types even when applied to inputs that may fall outside their intended domain; and a fine-grained analysis of guards that enables accurate type refinement for case expressions and guarded function definitions. While type information is erased before execution and not used by the compiler, our "safe erasure" gradual typing strategy maintains soundness and expressiveness without compromising compatibility or performance. This work lays the theoretical foundation for Elixir's new type system, outlines its integration into recent versions of the language, and demonstrates its effectiveness on large-scale industrial codebases.

title: STATIC: Surface-normal-guided Two-branch Alignment and Temporal Integration for Consistent Video Depth Estimation
summary: Video depth estimation is essential for applications such as autonomous driving, AR/VR, and robotics. Recent transformer-based single-image monocular depth estimation models perform well on a single image but struggle with depth consistency across video frames. Traditional methods aim to improve temporal consistency using multi-frame temporal modules or explicit priors like optical flow and camera parameters. However, these approaches face issues such as high memory use, reduced performance with dynamic or irregular motion, and a heavy reliance on the accuracy of external motion estimators. We propose STATIC, a novel model that independently learns temporal consistency in geometrically stable and unstable regions using only two adjacent frames. By leveraging intrinsic geometric cues rather than external motion priors, STATIC generates a depth-derived geometry-aware difference mask from surface normals to identify regions with inter-frame geometric variation by measuring directional variance. For geometrically stable regions, the Masked Stable (MS) module enhances temporal consistency by focusing on structurally stable regions. For geometrically unstable regions, the Surface Normal Similarity (SNS) module models inter-frame correspondences and ensures temporal consistency by measuring feature similarities between frames. A final refinement integrates the independently learned stable and unstable features, enabling STATIC to improve consistent depth prediction across consecutive frames. Experiments on KITTI, NYUv2, and Sintel demonstrate strong depth accuracy and temporal consistency, as well as stable performance across the tested frame-rate and camera-motion conditions.

title: MeshCone: Second-Order Cone Programming for Geometrically-Constrained Mesh Enhancement
comments: This submission has been withdrawn by the authors. Upon further review, we identified issues in the analysis that require significant revision. An updated and more thoroughly developed version will be submitted once these have been resolved
summary: Modern mesh generation pipelines whether learning-based or classical often produce outputs requiring post-processing to achieve production-quality geometry. This work introduces MeshCone, a convex optimization framework for guided mesh refinement that leverages reference geometry to correct deformed or degraded meshes. We formulate the problem as a second-order cone program where vertex positions are optimized to align with target geometry while enforcing smoothness through convex edge-length regularization. MeshCone performs geometry-aware optimization that preserves fine details while correcting structural defects. We demonstrate robust performance across 56 diverse object categories from ShapeNet and ThreeDScans, achieving superior refinement quality compared to Laplacian smoothing and unoptimized baselines while maintaining sub-second inference times. MeshCone is particularly suited for applications where reference geometry is available, such as mesh-from-template workflows, scan-to-CAD alignment, and quality assurance in asset production pipelines.

title: Power- and Fragmentation-aware Online Scheduling for GPU Datacenters
comments: Published in the proceedings of IEEE CCGrid 2025
summary: The rise of Artificial Intelligence and Large Language Models is driving increased GPU usage in data centers for complex training and inference tasks, impacting operational costs, energy demands, and the environmental footprint of large-scale computing infrastructures. This work addresses the online scheduling problem in GPU datacenters, which involves scheduling tasks without knowledge of their future arrivals. We focus on two objectives: minimizing GPU fragmentation and reducing power consumption. GPU fragmentation occurs when partial GPU allocations hinder the efficient use of remaining resources, especially as the datacenter nears full capacity. A recent scheduling policy, Fragmentation Gradient Descent (FGD), leverages a fragmentation metric to address this issue. Reducing power consumption is also crucial due to the significant power demands of GPUs. To this end, we propose PWR, a novel scheduling policy to minimize power usage by selecting power-efficient GPU and CPU combinations. This involves a simplified model for measuring power consumption integrated into a Kubernetes score plugin. Through an extensive experimental evaluation in a simulated cluster, we show how PWR, when combined with FGD, achieves a balanced trade-off between reducing power consumption and minimizing GPU fragmentation.
comment: Published in the proceedings of IEEE CCGrid 2025

title: Enhancing Table Recognition with Vision LLMs: A Benchmark and Neighbor-Guided Toolchain Reasoner
summary: Pre-trained foundation models have recently made significant progress in table-related tasks such as table understanding and reasoning. However, recognizing the structure and content of unstructured tables using Vision Large Language Models (VLLMs) remains under-explored. To bridge this gap, we propose a benchmark based on a hierarchical design philosophy to evaluate the recognition capabilities of VLLMs in training-free scenarios. Through in-depth evaluations, we find that low-quality image input is a significant bottleneck in the recognition process. Drawing inspiration from this, we propose the Neighbor-Guided Toolchain Reasoner (NGTR) framework, which is characterized by integrating diverse lightweight tools for visual operations aimed at mitigating issues with low-quality images. Specifically, we transfer a tool selection experience from a similar neighbor to the input and design a reflection module to supervise the tool invocation process. Extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly enhances the recognition capabilities of the vanilla VLLMs. We believe that the benchmark and framework could provide an alternative solution to table recognition.

title: Hierarchical Vision Transformer with Prototypes for Interpretable Medical Image Classification
summary: Explainability is an important requirement for machine learning models in high-risk domains such as medicine. We introduce HierViT, a hierarchical Vision Transformer that combines competitive predictive performance with multiple mechanisms to support the interpretation of its predictions. The model first predicts clinically relevant visual appearance attributes, which are then used to infer the final target prediction through a hierarchical reasoning process. To facilitate understanding of the intermediate representations, attribute-specific prototypes are visualized as representative image examples, while attribute-specific attention maps highlight image regions associated with each visual feature. Together, these attribute-level components provide complementary views of the model's reasoning by linking representative image examples and spatial attention to semantically defined visual features. We evaluate HierViT on two medical benchmark datasets: LIDC-IDRI for lung nodule assessment and derm7pt for skin lesion classification. Across both datasets, HierViT achieves competitive predictive performance while providing attribute-level prototypes and attention visualizations that support the interpretation of its predictions.

title: BeforeIT.jl: High-Performance Agent-Based Macroeconomics Made Easy
summary: BeforeIT is an open-source software for building and simulating state-of-the-art macroeconomic agent-based models (macro ABMs) based on the recently introduced macro ABM developed in [1] and here referred to as the base model. Written in Julia, it combines extraordinary computational efficiency with user-friendliness and extensibility. We present the main structure of the software, demonstrate its ease of use with illustrative examples, and benchmark its performance. Our benchmarks demonstrate that the base model built with BeforeIT is orders of magnitude faster than its original Matlab implementation, while achieving performance comparable to a highly optimised HPC implementation. Furthermore, we show how BeforeIT supports an easy construction of model variants such as the 'CANVAS' model of [2], how these variants can be evaluated at scale via an automated multicountry forecasting pipeline, and how the entire simulation can be automatically differentiated. BeforeIT is designed to facilitate reproducibility, extensibility, and experimentation. As the first open-source, industry-grade software to build macro ABMs, BeforeIT can significantly foster collaboration and innovation in the field of agent-based macroeconomic modelling. The package, along with its documentation, is freely available at https://github.com/bancaditalia/BeforeIT.jl under the Apache 2.0 license.

title: MouseGPT: A Large-scale Vision-Language Model for Mouse Behavior Analysis
comments: 74 pages, 5 main figures, 9 extended figures, 6 supplementary figures and 3 supplementary tables
summary: Analyzing animal behavior is crucial in neuroscience, yet deciphering its intricate dynamics remains challenging. Traditional machine vision approaches detect spontaneous behaviors but are constrained by limited interpretability and reliance on manual labeling, restricting exploration of the full behavioral spectrum. Here, we introduce MouseGPT, an integrated vision-language model and analytical framework that translates raw video of animal activity into natural language to automate open-vocabulary behavior analysis. Built upon a comprehensive dataset of over 42 million frames spanning diverse psychiatric conditions, MouseGPT maps multi-view or single-camera recordings directly into computable semantic representations. An agentic framework leverages these representations for detailed behavior profiling, cross-view stable clustering, and zero-shot novel behavior discovery without requiring labor-intensive annotation. Surpassing conventional kinematics-based pipelines and generalist vision-language models in behavioral precision and adaptability, MouseGPT establishes continuous semantic representations as a powerful tool for deciphering complex ethological dynamics in animal models.

title: Camera Movement Estimation and Path Correction using the Combination of Modified A-SIFT and Stereo System for 3D Modelling
comments: The manuscript is being withdrawn due to the need for substantial revisions and corrections to the current version. We apologize for any inconvenience caused to readers
summary: Creating accurate and efficient 3D models poses significant challenges, particularly in addressing large viewpoint variations, computational complexity, and alignment discrepancies. Efficient camera path generation can help resolve these issues. In this context, a modified version of the Affine Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (ASIFT) is proposed to extract more matching points with reduced computational overhead, ensuring an adequate number of inliers for precise camera rotation angle estimation. Additionally, a novel two-camera-based rotation correction model is introduced to mitigate small rotational errors, further enhancing accuracy. Furthermore, a stereo camera-based translation estimation and correction model is implemented to determine camera movement in 3D space by altering the Structure From Motion (SFM) model. Finally, the novel combination of ASIFT and two camera-based SFM models provides an accurate camera movement trajectory in 3D space. Experimental results show that the proposed camera movement approach achieves 99.9% accuracy compared to the actual camera movement path and outperforms state-of-the-art camera path estimation methods. By leveraging this accurate camera path, the system facilitates the creation of precise 3D models, making it a robust solution for applications requiring high fidelity and efficiency in 3D reconstruction.

title: Haptic bilateral teleoperation system for free-hand dental procedures
summary: Free-hand dental procedures are typically repetitive, time-consuming and require high precision and manual dexterity. Robots can play a key role in improving procedural accuracy and safety, enhancing patient comfort, and reducing operator workload. However, robotic solutions for free-hand procedures remain limited or completely lacking. To address this gap, we develop a haptic bilateral teleoperation system (HBTS) for free-hand dental procedures (FH-HBTS). The system includes a mechanical end-effector, compatible with standard clinical tools, and equipped with an endoscopic camera for improved visibility of the intervention site. By ensuring motion and force correspondence between the operator's and the robot's actions, monitored through visual feedback, we enhance the operator's sensory awareness and motor accuracy. Furthermore, to ensure procedural safety, we limit interaction forces by scaling the motion references provided to the admittance controller based solely on measured contact forces. This ensures effective force limitation in all contact states without requiring prior knowledge of the environment. The proposed FH-HBTS is validated through a technical evaluation and an in-vitro pre-clinical study conducted on a dental model under clinically representative, yet simplified, conditions. The results show that the system improves the naturalness, safety, and accuracy of teleoperation, highlighting its potential to enhance free-hand dental procedures.

title: Catastrophic Overfitting, Entropy Gap and Participation Ratio: A Noiseless $l^p$ Norm Solution for Fast Adversarial Training
summary: Adversarial training is a cornerstone of robust deep learning, but fast methods like the Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) often suffer from Catastrophic Overfitting (CO), where models become robust to single-step attacks but fail against multi-step variants. While existing solutions rely on noise injection, regularization, or gradient clipping, we propose a novel solution that purely controls the $l^p$ training norm to mitigate CO. Our study is motivated by the empirical observation that CO is more prevalent under the $l^{\infty}$ norm than the $l^2$ norm. Leveraging this insight, we develop a framework for generalized $l^p$ attack as a fixed point problem and craft $l^p$-FGSM attacks to understand the transition mechanics from $l^2$ to $l^{\infty}$. This leads to our core insight: CO emerges when highly concentrated gradients, where information localizes in few dimensions, interact with aggressive norm constraints. By quantifying gradient concentration through Participation Ratio and entropy measures, we develop an adaptive $l^p$-FGSM that automatically tunes the training norm based on gradient information. Extensive experiments demonstrate that this approach achieves competitive robustness without requiring additional regularization or noise injection, providing a novel and theoretically-principled pathway to mitigate the CO problem.

title: Deep Learning Warm Starts for Trajectory Optimization on the International Space Station
comments: International Conference on Space Robotics (iSpaRo) 2025. https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11436159 Earlier version presented at Workshop on Space Robotics at Robotics: Science and Systems (RSS) 2025
summary: Trajectory optimization is a cornerstone of modern robot autonomy, enabling systems to compute trajectories and controls in real-time while respecting safety and physical constraints. However, it has seen limited usage in spaceflight applications due to its heavy computational demands that exceed the capability of most flight computers. In this work, we provide results on the first in-space demonstration of using machine learning-based warm starts for accelerating trajectory optimization for the Astrobee free-flying robot onboard the International Space Station (ISS). We formulate a data-driven optimal control approach that trains a neural network to learn the structure of the trajectory generation problem being solved using sequential convex programming (SCP). Onboard, this trained neural network predicts solutions for the trajectory generation problem and relies on using the SCP solver to enforce safety constraints for the system. Our trained network reduces the number of solver iterations required for convergence in cases including rotational dynamics by 60% and in cases with obstacles drawn from the training distribution of the warm start model by 50%. This work represents a significant milestone in the use of learning-based control for spaceflight applications and a stepping stone for future advances in the use of machine learning for autonomous guidance, navigation, & control.

title: MEDMKG: Benchmarking Medical Knowledge Exploitation with Multimodal Knowledge Graph
summary: Medical deep learning models depend heavily on domain-specific knowledge to perform well on knowledge-intensive clinical tasks. Prior work has primarily leveraged unimodal knowledge graphs, such as the Unified Medical Language System (UMLS), to enhance model performance. However, integrating multimodal medical knowledge graphs remains largely underexplored, mainly due to the lack of resources linking imaging data with clinical concepts. To address this gap, we propose MEDMKG, a Medical Multimodal Knowledge Graph that unifies visual and textual medical information through a multi-stage construction pipeline. MEDMKG fuses the rich multimodal data from MIMIC-CXR with the structured clinical knowledge from UMLS, utilizing both rule-based tools and large language models for accurate concept extraction and relationship modeling. To ensure graph quality and compactness, we introduce Neighbor-aware Filtering (NaF), a novel filtering algorithm tailored for multimodal knowledge graphs. We evaluate MEDMKG across three tasks under two experimental settings, benchmarking twenty-four baseline methods and four state-of-the-art vision-language backbones on six datasets. Results show that MEDMKG not only improves performance in downstream medical tasks but also offers a strong foundation for developing adaptive and robust strategies for multimodal knowledge integration in medical artificial intelligence.

title: A Decision Procedure for Probabilistic Kleene Algebra with Angelic Nondeterminism
summary: In Ong et al.~(2025), a new finite automaton model with probabilistic and nondeterministic transitions was introduced, along with a corresponding regular expression language. The key difference from previous approaches is that nondeterminism is formalized in terms of multisets instead of powersets. Automata and expressions are interpreted over the space of probability distributions over multisets of strings with finite multiplicities. The main result of that paper was a full Kleene theorem showing that the two formalisms are equally expressive. In this paper we give a decision procedure for the semantic equivalence of two automata or expressions. The algorithm is based on polyomial algebra and makes use of Gröbner basis techniques for ideal membership testing.

title: From Dueling Bandits to Episodic MDPs: Learning with Adversarial Preference Feedback
summary: In dueling bandits, the learner compares two arms in each round and observes only which one is preferred. This paper asks what changes when the compared pair also affects the next state, as in a recommendation interface where the pair shown to a user affects the user's next context. We formulate this problem as a state-wise preference-based MDP, an episodic tabular MDP in which the learner selects a pair of arms at each visited state, observes only a noisy comparison between them, and moves to a next state that may depend on the pair. The preferences may change adversarially across episodes, and the loss of a pair is defined through Borda scores. We show that the minimax regret of this problem under known transitions is $\tildeΘ(\min\{HT,(H^3SK)^{1/3}T^{2/3}\})$, where $H$, $S$, $K$, and $T$ are the numbers of steps per episode, states, arms, and episodes, and that this rate is achieved by an algorithm based on online linear optimization over the set of occupancy measures. If the pair did not affect the next state, each state would be a separate dueling bandit, and the $T^{2/3}$ term of the minimax regret would be smaller by a factor of $H^{1/3}$, demonstrating the cost of having action-dependent state transitions. We also give a policy optimization algorithm with closed-form updates, whose regret is $\tilde{O}((H^4SK^3)^{1/3}T^{2/3})$ up to lower-order terms, and we extend both algorithms to unknown transitions.

title: A survey of diversity quantification in natural language processing: The why, what, where and how
summary: The concept of diversity received increasing attention in natural language processing (NLP) in recent years. It became an advocated property of datasets and systems, with many measures used to quantify it, but also many cross-paper inconsistencies. To address this fragmentation, we take inspiration from other scientific fields where diversity has been more thoroughly conceptualized. We build upon (Sarkar, 2010) and (Stirling, 2007), two unified cross-domain frameworks inspired from ecology, economy and other domains. The first one advocates explicit justification of diversity endorsement. The latter distinguishes three dimensions of diversity: variety, balance, and disparity. Surveying over 300 recent diversity-related papers from ACL Anthology, we propose an NLP-specific framework with 4 perspectives: why diversity is important, what diversity is measured on, where it is measured, and how. We find that in NLP richness (the simplest variety) and distance averaging (the simplest disparity) are the most prevalent measure families, and that pure balance measures are nearly absent. Moreover, half of the measures used in NLP do not conform to Stirling's framework. Our analysis increases comparability of approaches to diversity in NLP, allowing us to formulate recommendations for the field. We recommend that the field systematically use a unified terminology, and that it engage in debates about the desirable properties of diversity measures as well as about the normative assumptions behind their use.

title: NS-Net: Decoupling CLIP Semantic Information through NULL-Space for Generalizable AI-Generated Image Detection
summary: The rapid progress of generative models, such as GANs and diffusion models, has facilitated the creation of highly realistic images, raising growing concerns over their misuse in security-sensitive domains. While existing detectors perform well under known generative settings, they often fail to generalize to unknown generative models, especially when semantic content between real and fake images is closely aligned. In this paper, we revisit the use of CLIP features for AI-generated image detection and uncover a critical limitation: the high-level semantic information embedded in CLIP's visual features hinders effective discrimination. To address this, we propose the NS-Net, a novel detection framework that leverages NULL-Space projection to decouple semantic information from CLIP's visual features, followed by contrastive learning to capture intrinsic distributional differences between real and generated images. Furthermore, we design a Patch Selection strategy to preserve fine-grained artifacts by selecting patches with the highest and lowest spectral entropy. Extensive experiments on an open-world benchmark comprising images generated by 47 diverse generative models show that NS-Net outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 5.0\% improvement in detection accuracy, thereby demonstrating strong generalization across both GAN- and diffusion-based image generation techniques. Our code is available at https://github.com/HorizonTEL/NS-Net.

title: Bistatic Target Detection by Exploiting Both Deterministic Pilots and Unknown Random Data Payloads
comments: Integrated sensing and communications, bistatic target detection, random signals, false alarm probability, detection probability
summary: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) plays a crucial role in 6G, enabling innovative applications such as drone surveillance, urban air mobility, and low-altitude logistics. However, the hybrid ISAC signal, which comprises deterministic pilot and random data payload components, poses challenges for target detection due to two reasons: 1) these two components cause coupled shifts in both the mean and variance of the received signal, and 2) the random data payloads are typically unknown to the sensing receiver in the bistatic setting. Unfortunately, these challenges could not be tackled by existing target detection algorithms. In this paper, a generalized likelihood ratio test (GLRT)-based detector is derived by leveraging the known deterministic pilots and the statistical characteristics of the unknown random data payloads. Due to the analytical intractability of exact performance characterization, we perform an asymptotic analysis for the false alarm probability and detection probability of the proposed detector. The results reveal a deterministic-random trade-off: the deterministic pilots enhance detection through a target-induced mean shift, while the random data payloads provide an additional covariance-domain target signature but simultaneously introduce statistical uncertainty due to their unknown realizations. Simulations validate the theoretical findings and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed detector, which highlights the necessity of designing a dedicated detector to fully exploit the signaling resources assigned to random data payloads.
